text: Course 11 covered active-active and active-passive as two patterns you choose between, driven by RTO and RPO. That reasoning still holds, but it was built around a single workload. At enterprise scale you're not protecting one app — you're protecting dozens of interdependent services, and the coordination problem that creates doesn't just add up, it multiplies.

The first thing that has to change is the assumption that one pattern covers the whole estate. A payments ledger with a seconds-level RTO justifies active-active. An internal reporting tool with a days-level RTO doesn't need any standing DR capacity at all. Real enterprise DR architecture is a mix of patterns applied per workload tier, with services grouped into failover domains so the ones that depend on each other move together instead of independently.

Here's what that tiering actually looks like written down: the payments ledger runs active-active because its RTO is seconds and its RPO is effectively zero. Checkout and pricing run as a warm standby because minutes and sub-minute loss are tolerable. Search and recommendations can live on a cold, backup-restore posture because hours of downtime genuinely don't hurt the business. Reporting waits a day. Each tier gets the pattern its own numbers justify, not the pattern that feels the most resilient on a diagram.

The real complexity shows up at the boundary between tiers. Say checkout is active-active across two regions, but it calls a pricing service that's only active-passive with one primary. When the primary region fails, checkout is already serving fine from the second region — but if pricing hasn't promoted its standby yet, checkout is now making calls into a dead region. Checkout's real-world RTO was never just its own; it's bounded by the slowest dependency it calls during a failover.

That's the problem the next lesson solves directly: you can't reason about blast radius, or keep dependent services failing over together, until you actually know what depends on what. Next, building a real dependency map — a service catalog and dependency graph — so a failover decision accounts for everything actually affected, not just the one service that obviously went down.
